content: 1. Studies have shown that the Ebola virus experiences a significant decline in survival within sewage environments, with a 99.9995% reduction observed over the course of one month. 2. In comparison, coronaviruses were found to be non-recoverable after just one day in similar conditions. 3. A 99% reduction in coronavirus infectivity was achieved within two days at 30°C and six days at 22°C, indicating a relatively short survival period for enveloped viruses like Ebola. 4. Researchers suggest that enveloped viruses can undergo a 6–7 log10 reduction in sewage within 3–7 days, depending on the temperature. 5. Non-enveloped viruses, such as poliovirus, exhibit a much slower decline in survival, with only a 9% reduction over one month, highlighting the greater resilience of non-enveloped pathogens. 6. This equates to a 3–5 log greater decline in Ebola virus survival compared to poliovirus under similar conditions. 7. Ongoing studies are investigating the survival of Ebola virus in fecal matter, with one recent publication providing insights into its persistence. 8. Field studies in West Africa are also examining the presence and survival of the virus in fecal masses contained within pit latrines. 9. As new evidence emerges, it will be disseminated, and recommendations will be updated accordingly. 10. Ebola virus and other filoviruses are highly susceptible to a wide range of disinfectants and chemical agents, including domestic bleach, sodium hypochlorite, calcium hypochlorite, and organic solvents. 11. The precautionary principle emphasizes the need for meticulous care during the decontamination of Ebola care facilities to ensure the safety of both the decommissioning team and the public. 12. Where evidence is limited, the precautionary principle has been applied to guide safe practices in decommissioning activities. 13. Community engagement is a critical component of the decommissioning process for Ebola care facilities. 14. This involves recognizing the community's leadership, culture, and concerns, and adopting appropriate approaches to educate, interact, and collaborate with them. 15. Discussions with the community should address their views on the decommissioning process, safety, health, and environmental concerns, as well as their role in supporting safe decommissioning efforts. 16. The decommissioning process for Ebola care facilities involves four key phases: preparation, decontamination, dismantling/repurposing, and reporting. 17. Preparation includes planning preand post-decontamination actions, maintaining access control, briefing the decommissioning team, and engaging with the community to inform and reassure them about the process. 18. Decontamination requires monitoring sectioned areas, demarcating zones, and ensuring proper cleaning and disinfection under the supervision of an Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) officer. 19. Dismantling involves the disassembly of temporary infrastructures, with materials either reused, recycled, or disposed of according to safety guidelines. 20. Reporting entails documenting all activities, waste management processes, and final recommendations, with a comprehensive report submitted within two weeks of completing the decommissioning process. 21. Infection prevention and control (IPC) principles are essential for terminal cleaning and decontamination of Ebola care facilities. 22. The Ebola virus is relatively fragile, with its infectivity rapidly declining outside its host due to its enveloped nature and susceptibility to disinfectants such as chlorine, ethanol, and ultraviolet light. 23. A trained IPC officer should oversee the inspection and supervision of the facility before, during, and after the decontamination process. 24. A checklist of necessary steps for cleaning, disinfection, and waste management should be developed and strictly followed to ensure safe and effective decontamination.
